t.1.47.1: Having spoken thus, O brahmin, the glorious lord of the earth, the tiger among the Bharatas, King Pārikṣita, approved by his ministers, then took upon himself the vow to perform the snake sacrifice.
t.1.47.2: Then the lord of the earth, accomplished in speech, summoned his family priest, the officiating priest, and spoke words meant to bring about the accomplishment of his purpose.
t.1.47.3: That evil-souled Takṣaka who killed my father, tell me, sirs, how I may take revenge on him.
t.1.47.4: Is that rite known to you, sirs, by which I shall cast the serpent Takṣaka, together with his kin, into the blazing fire?
t.1.47.5: Just as my father was formerly burned by him with the fire of his poison, so I too wish to burn that wicked serpent.
t.1.47.6: There is, O king, a great sacrificial session fashioned by the gods for your sake, renowned as the Serpent Sacrifice; it is told of in the Purāṇa, O lord of men.
t.1.47.7: “There is no performer of that sacrifice other than you, O lord of men”: so the knowers of ancient lore have declared, and that rite is ours to perform.
t.1.47.9: Then the king spoke to those brāhmaṇas versed in mantras: "I shall undertake that sacrificial session; let the requisites be gathered for me."
t.1.47.8: Thus addressed, that royal sage deemed the serpent Takṣaka as having indeed already entered the blazing mouth of the fire, O best of the virtuous.
t.1.47.10: Then, O best of brahmins, the priests of that king, who was duly versed in knowledge, measured out that ground according to the scriptures for the making of the sacrificial enclosure, all of them having reached the highest through their understanding.
t.1.47.12: And having duly constructed the desired sacrificial ground according to the rules, they then consecrated the king for the undertaking of the snake sacrifice.
t.1.47.11: Endowed with supreme splendour, the sacrifice was thronged with hosts of twice-born, rich in abundant wealth and grain, and well laid out by the officiating priests.
t.1.47.14: While that site for the sacrifice was being prepared, the master builder, endowed with intelligence and skilled in the science of building, spoke these words.
t.1.47.13: And this happened there beforehand, concerning the snake sacrifice that was to take place: a great portent arose at that time, one that would bring about an obstruction of the sacrifice.
t.1.47.15: Then the architect, a Sūta versed in the Purāṇas, spoke thus: “Because of the place and the time at which this measuring out was begun, this sacrifice will not reach completion, a brahmin being made the cause.”
t.1.47.17: Then the rite of the snake sacrifice commenced according to the prescribed ordinance, and the officiating priests moved about duly, each in his own appointed task.
t.1.47.16: Having heard this, the king, before the time of his consecration, said to the doorkeeper: “Let no one unknown to me enter here.”
t.1.47.18: Having put on black garments, their eyes reddened by the smoke, they made offerings, with the proper mantras, into the kindled Jātavedas.
t.1.47.19: And they, making the minds of all the serpents tremble, then offered all the snakes there as oblations into the mouth of the fire.
t.1.47.20: Then the serpents fell into the blazing fire, writhing in misery and calling out to one another.
t.1.47.21: Others, writhing and hissing and coiling about with their tails and heads, violently fell into the bright-flamed fire, Citrabhānu.
t.1.47.22: White, black and blue ones, old and young alike, uttering cries out of terror, fell into the blazing fire.
t.1.47.23: Thus hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of serpents perished helplessly, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.47.25: Many serpents, high and low, of various colours and swollen with venom, terrible, resembling iron clubs, biting and of great strength, fell into the fire, tormented by the rod of their mother's curse.
t.1.47.24: Some there were like rats, others like the trunks of elephants, and others like rutting elephants, huge of body and of great strength.
